note: DESIGN §3.7's human comp-approval gate, as a ledger instead of prose. HAND-EDITED — the capture script never writes this file, and `approve.mjs` only records rulings. `test/comps-captures.test.js` enforces its shape, its coverage of every (state × viewport) §3.7 names, that each entry's `frame` is a comp frame that ACTUALLY EXISTS in the named file, that both compare frames render two WHOLE panels with a distinct agent in each pane on the axis §2.5 specifies for their viewport (side-by-side at ≥900px, a stacked pair below the 900px breakpoint — the operator's 2026-07-30 amendment, which is itself asserted against DESIGN §2.5 so the comps cannot drift ahead of the spec), that no comp draws a death time §6.2 cannot supply, and that `entryGate` below tells the truth about the rulings. It cannot enforce the rulings themselves: approval is the human reviewer's act, and a test that manufactured it would defeat the gate.
provenance: W8a's sign-off predates this file and was recorded only in prose (comps/README.md, built/README.md). The `approved` entries below transcribe it: the W8 entry gate ruled on the W8a comp set, which was authored at 1440 throughout — DESIGN.md:350, :362 and :437 carry amendments made *per that ruling*, which is the evidence that it happened. Per-frame records were not kept then; from W8b round 5 on, this file is where a ruling is recorded, and an entry with no `decidedBy` has not been ruled on.
conformanceEdits: W8c corrected seven 9px type declarations in the comp stylesheet to §3.1's 11px floor (§3.2 reserves 9px for the `.ad` adapter monogram, and none of the nine approved deviations D1–D9 is a typography change). Those edits touch every frame, including approved ones, and they do NOT re-open a ruling: approving a comp cannot license a violation of §3.1, so restoring conformance restores what was approved rather than changing it. `test/comps-type-scale.test.js` now runs the same validator the product uses over `docs/frontend/comps/lib`, so the two stylesheets cannot drift apart again. Two frames DID change substantively and are re-opened below, each with its own `why`.
entryGate: PASSED — all 8 of §3.7's compositions (four canonical states × two viewports) are approved. The most recent ruling was recorded by Ben Vargas (operator) in the §3.7 gate ruling, via the flowition ask/answer channel — VARIANT B, the stacked pair, chosen over the side-by-side alternative; DESIGN §2.5 amended accordingly (side-by-side normative at >=900px, stacked pair below the 900px breakpoint). Each entry carries its own decidedBy/decidedIn.

supportingFrames: Four frames in this directory are NOT §3.7 compositions and carry no ledger entry, because §3.7 names 1440 and 800 and this file may not invent a third required viewport. They exist because §3.3's rule ("below 900px the rails collapse into drawers and the transcript replaces the cockpit") needs a floor and an open state to be buildable: `cockpit.html` → "the run rail OPEN as a drawer (scrim + focus model)" and "at 480px"; `transcript.html` → "replaces the cockpit at 800px" and "at 480px"; `home.html` → "Home — 480px". They are annotated like any other frame and the operator may rule on them in the same sitting, but they do not gate W8.

compositions.why: This entry moved BACKWARDS, from approved to pending, in W8c. W8a's ruling approved a stale attention card reading "Engine died 26m ago" with a 21m18s runtime beside it. Neither figure exists: `endedAt` is written from a terminal `run` event and from nothing else (§6.2, src/viewer/summaries.js:115-118), and a run is `stale` precisely because the engine went away WITHOUT writing one. The comp was deriving the death time from the run's age (and elsewhere from the `run.lock` mtime, which dates when the engine ACQUIRED the run). The shipped Home already renders this honestly — AttentionStrip.tsx: "It wrote no terminal event, so there is no time of death to report" — so the approved comp contradicted its OWN committed built captures, which are the §3.7 side-by-side evidence for this very entry. The card now states what it knows and the runtime figure is gone with it. That is a change to what the screen says, not a stylesheet correction, so the old ruling does not carry.
decide: annotation 11 — the stale card states the time of death as UNKNOWN and reports the start time instead, rather than dating the death from startedAt or the run.lock mtime. The alternative is a W6 change adding an authoritative `lastSeenAt` to RunSummary, which would let the card carry a real number
annotation 11 — the elapsed figure ("21m18s") is dropped from the stale card entirely, because elapsed(startedAt, null, now) counts upward forever on a run that stopped

annotations 1-7 — unchanged from the W8a ruling (the three-card attention strip, the single accent action, the budget gauge on Home, filter chips, blank-not-zero, older-engine badges, 44px density). Re-confirm or restate

All three steers read `queued` and two say `no callsite journalled`. Both are FACTS OF THE FIXTURE, not of the UI: the mock adapter's sleeper takes steers as queued follow-up turns, and the operator's `flowition send` carries no workflow source position — only the workflow's own sendTo() does, and its callsite is on screen. The comp draws a `dropped` verdict in red; the product renders that class (`.verdict.dropped`) and cockpit.test.tsx covers it.

The panel's three judges are ECHO agents that finish in ~0ms, so their bars are marks rather than the comp's wide bands, and no agent is quiet long enough for the amber Q2 tag. The comp's world is a 14-minute run; the fixture's is a 25-second one.

Cost reads `not journalled` and no log line is present: the mock adapter prices nothing and these workflows never call log(). §2.3's "empty ≠ zero" (parity #53/#114) forbids fabricating $0.00, and parity #59's row states the absence.

compositions.frame: Two-panel compare at 800px (§3.7's second required viewport)
compositions.why: Comped in round 5 as a tablist (a switcher — correctly rejected), REDRAWN in round 6 as a vertical stack, REDRAWN AGAIN in W8c as the side-by-side pair §2.5 then specified, with the stack kept beside it as VARIANT B. This was the one slot in the set where the operator was asked to CHOOSE between two drawings rather than confirm one, because adopting the stack meant amending a normative sentence and an implementation lane cannot do that. THE OPERATOR CHOSE VARIANT B. The stacked pair is now the composition this entry names, the side-by-side drawing is retained in transcript.html as ALTERNATIVE A (considered, not chosen), and DESIGN §2.5 carries the amendment as a marked operator ruling: side-by-side stays normative at ≥900px, and below §3.3's 900px breakpoint the compare renders as a stacked pair (full-width panels, sequential scroll).
compositions.ruling: VARIANT B — the stacked pair. Recorded by Ben Vargas via the flowition ask/answer channel, together with the DESIGN §2.5 amendment that the choice required. The reason on the record: at 800px both rails are 44px handles, so side by side each pane is ~355px, under the 607px the row types were designed at — the same row then wraps differently on the two sides, and the operator is comparing two renderings rather than two answers. The stack keeps both panes at the full 712px and spends scrollback depth instead, which annotation 12's shared pin bar buys back by anchoring both panes to the same step. W10 builds the stacked form below 900px; the ≥900px composition (transcript-compare-1440) is unchanged.
decide: THE VARIANT CHOICE — annotations 11 and 18. (A) the side-by-side pair: two ~355px panes, each with a 340px minimum so a narrower viewport scrolls the PAIR horizontally rather than degrading into a switcher; the cost is that the facts row wraps, the gutter narrows 56 → 40px, and cards wrap where the 1440 frame does not. (B) the stacked pair: both panes at the full 712px so a row renders identically in both, ~370px of height each, and §2.5 needs an amendment recorded in DESIGN. RULED: (B), with the §2.5 amendment made

annotation 12 — the shared pin bar (both panes anchored to the same step, plus the output-token delta) as the thing that keeps two short/narrow panes showing the same moment. Identical in both drawings; load-bearing in the chosen one, since stacked panes are never at eye level together
annotation 13 — the rails as 44px handles, matching the cockpit at 800 rather than a second idiom

annotation 17 — the seam between panes heavier than any rule inside a pane, so one agent's rows cannot be read as the other's. Stacked, the two panes share a column, a width and an edge, so the seam is 2px hairline-strong rather than a hairline
